title: Potted Shrimps
subtitle: Small brown shrimps set in spiced butter, served with toast
excerpt: Tiny brown shrimps suspended in spiced butter with mace, cayenne, and nutmeg, chilled until set and turned out onto hot buttered toast. A classic British seafood starter that takes 15 minutes to make.
sourceNotes: Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), potted shrimps with mace and cayenne, served cold on toast. Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Potted shrimps from Morecambe Bay, Lancashire, have been a documented British delicacy since at least the seventeenth century.

recipe.batchNotes: Scale freely. Make up to 3 days ahead and keep covered in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Must be made at least 1 hour ahead to allow the butter to set. Keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days.

content.text: Potted shrimps are small cooked shrimps set in spiced clarified butter, chilled until firm, then turned out and eaten on hot toast. The butter melts on contact with the warm toast and releases the sweet, maritime flavour of the shrimps. Use the smallest shrimps you can find: the traditional choice is Morecambe Bay brown shrimps, sold peeled and ready.

items.prepNote: small brown shrimps or peeled cooked prawns
slices, toasted and buttered, to serve

content.text: Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over low heat. Add {{mace-ground}} of ground mace, {{cayenne-pepper}} of cayenne, a small grating of nutmeg, and the juice of {{lemon}}. Stir gently.
Add {{prawns-cooked}} of shrimps or peeled prawns to the butter. Warm through over very low heat for 2 minutes. Do not let the butter boil. Taste and adjust the seasoning.
Divide between 4 ramekins or small pots, making sure each gets an equal amount of shrimps. Pour the spiced butter over the top to cover.
Refrigerate for at least 1 hour until the butter is completely set. To serve, run a knife around the edge of each pot and turn out onto plates. Serve immediately with hot buttered toast.

rows.symptom: Butter is grainy rather than smooth
rows.cause: Butter separated or boiled during heating
rows.fix: Melt the butter slowly over the lowest possible heat. It should never bubble.

rows.cause: Not enough spice or no acid
rows.fix: Taste the spiced butter before adding the shrimps. It should be noticeably spiced. Add more mace and cayenne if needed, and make sure the lemon juice is in.

rows.cause: Heated too long or at too high a temperature
rows.fix: The shrimps only need 2 minutes in warm butter. They are already cooked: you are just warming them through and coating them.

rows.cause: Not enough butter relative to shrimps, or fridge not cold enough
rows.fix: Ensure the butter covers the shrimps completely. If the pot is in the fridge door where it is warmer, move it to a shelf.

content.text: Potted shrimps are most associated with Morecambe Bay on the Lancashire coast, where brown shrimps have been fished, boiled, and potted in spiced butter since at least the seventeenth century. The Baxter family in Morecambe has been potting shrimps commercially since 1799. The dish is now sold in fishmongers and delis across Britain. It is one of the oldest continuously-made British convenience foods: a preserved seafood product designed to be eaten cold on toast, requiring no cooking at the table.
